Historical findings CASEID FILE NOTE
1) Domain context: An institutional records office files ordinary paperwork as dated documents with labeled fields, routes them through named channels to specific accounts, and retains each submission under a reference number for later retrieval. Entries are indexed by actor, date, and channel, and retained copies remain in the archive for audit review.

2) What occurred: The actor submitted a single ticket document tied to a named account and a dated record. The actor generated multiple duplicate documents carrying the same event, seat, and barcode fields. The actor transmitted those duplicate documents through a named resale channel to several buyer accounts. The actor arranged for one buyer account to present its document at the gate before the other documents were presented. The actor submitted a refund request through a support channel, reversed the request, and later filed a chargeback notice with a named payment processor. The actor collected buyer identity details into a contact list within the same account.

3) Materials/access observed: One source ticket document with an event name, date, seat, and machine-readable field; four duplicate documents sharing those fields; a resale channel listing document; a gate presentation record; a support-channel transcript with a refund request and reversal; a payment-processor chargeback notice; and a contact list holding buyer names and identifiers, all associated with the named account.

4) Indicators & artifacts: Identical event, seat, and barcode fields across multiple documents; a single source document referenced by several resale listings; a gate presentation record for one document preceding the others; a refund request in the support transcript followed by its reversal; a chargeback notice filed with a payment processor after the refund request; a contact list aggregating buyer identifiers within the named account; and timestamp gaps between document creation, resale submission, and gate presentation.
